site.name: lumen-research
site.summary: Lumen Research — research assistant (local demo) Fictional research-assistant chat product. Local fixture for UXBench. Open `index.html` directly. Page `index.html` — Research thread Three-column layout: left rail for thread history, center conversation, right rail for Sources. Center column: - Conversation styled with serif body type. Each assistant turn renders inline citations as small chips (`[1]`, `[2]` …). Hovering a citation highlights and scrolls the matching source on the right; clicking jumps to it. - Embedded tables and lists are styled with the rest of the conversation.

run_plan.goal: Evaluate the UX of the Lumen Research chatbot interface, focusing on the core conversation flow, citation/source interaction mechanics, and responsive layout stability.
run_plan.summary: The exploration will proceed by first validating the primary 'Ask' loop and response rendering. It will then stress-test the unique 'citation-to-source' linking mechanism (hover/click) and the right-rail filtering controls. Finally, it will assess mobile responsiveness, specifically targeting the identified small tap targets in the left navigation rail.
assumptions: The application is a single-page local fixture (`index.html`) where state changes (new threads, mode switches) are handled via JavaScript without full page reloads.
The 'Sources' panel content updates dynamically based on the active conversation turn or selected filters.
The 'Mode' dropdowns control the persona or depth of the AI response generation.
risk_hotspots: Citation Chips ([1], [2]): Interaction logic for highlighting corresponding sources in the right rail.
Left Rail Navigation: Identified small tap targets (<44px height) posing mobile usability risks.
Mode Selectors: Ambiguity between the top-right global mode and the bottom-right input-area mode.
Input Area: Textarea expansion behavior and attachment button functionality.

phases.title: Core Conversation & Input Loop
phases.objective: Validate the primary user journey: composing queries, submitting them, and receiving formatted responses.
key_checks: Submit a new query via the textarea and 'Ask' button to verify response generation.
Test the 'Quick scan' vs 'Deep dive' modes in the bottom-right selector to observe response differences.
Verify the 'Attach' (paperclip) button state and any resulting file picker or UI change.
Check if suggested follow-up buttons (e.g., 'Power analysis...') correctly inject text into the input field.
exit_criteria: Successful submission of at least one new message.
Visible change in UI or response style when toggling input modes.

phases.title: Citation & Source Mechanics
phases.objective: Stress-test the unique value proposition: the link between inline citations and the source panel.
key_checks: Hover over inline citation chips (e.g., `[1]`, `[4]`) to verify the corresponding source highlights in the right rail.
Click a citation chip to test scroll-to-source behavior.
Interact with Right Rail filters ('All', 'Papers', 'Books') to ensure the list updates correctly.
Change the 'Sort: Relevance' dropdown to check for re-ordering of sources.
exit_criteria: Confirmed visual feedback (highlight/scroll) on citation interaction.
Source list correctly filters/sorts based on right-rail controls.

phases.title: Thread Management & Global Controls
phases.objective: Explore adjacent flows involving history management and export features.
key_checks: Click '+ New thread' to verify canvas clearing and state reset.
Navigate to a previous thread from the Left Rail (e.g., 'EV battery recycling...') to check state restoration.
Test 'Share thread' and 'Export as PDF' buttons for modal triggers or download behaviors.
Toggle the top-right 'Mode: Balanced' selector to see if it affects the whole session context.
exit_criteria: New thread starts with a clean slate.
Old threads load their respective history and sources accurately.

phases.title: Mobile Responsiveness & Accessibility
phases.objective: Validate layout integrity on mobile viewports, focusing on known layout warnings.
key_checks: Switch to mobile viewport (e.g., iPhone SE/Pixel 5).
Attempt to tap Left Rail items (identified as <44px height) to assess touch target difficulty.
Check for overlap between the fixed header/footer and the main conversation content.
Verify if the three-column layout collapses gracefully (e.g., into tabs or drawers) or breaks.
exit_criteria: Documentation of specific tap-target failures in the left rail.
Confirmation that core chat functionality remains accessible despite layout shifts.

coverage_targets.pages: 100% of `index.html` interactive states (since it is a SPA).
coverage_targets.features: Exercise all 14 buttons, 4 inputs, and both select dropdowns visible in the prescan.
coverage_targets.mobile: Repeat Phase 1 and Phase 2 checks on a narrow viewport (<600px width).

notes: The prescan flagged multiple 'small_tap_target' warnings in the left sidebar; prioritize these in the mobile phase.
There are two 'Mode' selectors (top right and bottom right); clarify if they serve different functions (global vs. per-message).
Since this is a local demo, network errors are not expected, but console JS errors during state transitions should be monitored.

observation.title: Lumen Research — research assistant
observation.visible_text: Lumen + New thread TODAY Deep work scheduling literature EV battery recycling policy in Norway Trace prevalence of seal influenza H10N7 LAST 7 DAYS Comparative grad-school stipends in CS Microclimate effects of urban rooftop gardens Late-Holocene shoreline shifts, NW Europe Why does ringing happen in step responses EARLIER Survey: open-source funding models 2024 Caffeine half-life in slow metabolizers Building codes vs wildfire defensible space PA Priya Anand Researcher · Pro Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." 📎 Balanced Quick scan Deep dive Ask Follow-up questions Lumen suggests Find papers since 2020 directly comparing the two schedules Power analysis for 24 engineers × 2 weeks Surface negative results: where mornings didn't help Walk me through pre-registering on OSF Sources 8 Sort: Relevance Sort: Date Sort: Cited in this answer All Papers Books Web Preprints N Chronotype distribution in working adults — a meta-analysis Nature Sci Reports · 2021 · Olszewski et al. 0.88 "...approximately 31% of respondents in industrialized settings scored as evening-type or strongly evening-type, with mean peak alertnes

observation.title: Lumen Research — research assistant
observation.visible_text: Lumen + New thread TODAY Deep work scheduling literature EV battery recycling policy in Norway Trace prevalence of seal influenza H10N7 LAST 7 DAYS Comparative grad-school stipends in CS Microclimate effects of urban rooftop gardens Late-Holocene shoreline shifts, NW Europe Why does ringing happen in step responses EARLIER Survey: open-source funding models 2024 Caffeine half-life in slow metabolizers Building codes vs wildfire defensible space PA Priya Anand Researcher · Pro Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." Can you summarize the key findings from the Newport & Hempel study mentioned in point 3? L Thinking out loud while I assemble sources… Here's a first pass. The most directly relevant body of work is the chronotype × intervention literature; I'll prioritize that and bring in a couple of negative results to keep the picture honest. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." Can you summarize the key findings from the Newport & Hempel study mentioned in point 3? L Thinking out loud while I assemble sources… Here's a first pass. L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." Can you summarize the key findings from the Newport & Hempel study mentioned in point 3? L Thinking out loud while I assemble sources… Here's a first pass. The most directly relevant body of work is the chronotype × intervention literature; I'll prioritize that and bring in a couple of negative results to keep the picture honest. observation.visible_text: Lumen + New thread TODAY Deep work scheduling literature EV battery recycling policy in Norway Trace prevalence of seal influenza H10N7 LAST 7 DAYS Comparative grad-school stipends in CS Microclimate effects of urban rooftop gardens Late-Holocene shoreline shifts, NW Europe Why does ringing happen in step responses EARLIER Survey: open-source funding models 2024 Caffeine half-life in slow metabolizers Building codes vs wildfire defensible space PA Priya Anand Researcher · Pro Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." Can you summarize the key findings from the Newport & Hempel study mentioned in point 3? L Thinking out loud while I assemble sources… Here's a first pass. The most directly relevant body of work is the chronotype × intervention literature; I'll prioritize that and bring in a couple of negative results to keep the picture honest. observation.visible_text: Lumen + New thread TODAY Deep work scheduling literature EV battery recycling policy in Norway Trace prevalence of seal influenza H10N7 LAST 7 DAYS Comparative grad-school stipends in CS Microclimate effects of urban rooftop gardens Late-Holocene shoreline shifts, NW Europe Why does ringing happen in step responses EARLIER Survey: open-source funding models 2024 Caffeine half-life in slow metabolizers Building codes vs wildfire defensible space PA Priya Anand Researcher · Pro Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." Can you summarize the key findings from the Newport & Hempel study mentioned in point 3? L Thinking out loud while I assemble sources… Here's a first pass. The most directly relevant body of work is the chronotype × intervention literature; I'll prioritize that and bring in a couple of negative results to keep the picture honest. observation.title: Lumen Research — research assistant
observation.visible_text: Lumen + New thread TODAY Deep work scheduling literature EV battery recycling policy in Norway Trace prevalence of seal influenza H10N7 LAST 7 DAYS Comparative grad-school stipends in CS Microclimate effects of urban rooftop gardens Late-Holocene shoreline shifts, NW Europe Why does ringing happen in step responses EARLIER Survey: open-source funding models 2024 Caffeine half-life in slow metabolizers Building codes vs wildfire defensible space PA Priya Anand Researcher · Pro Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." Can you summarize the key findings from the Newport & Hempel study mentioned in point 3? L Thinking out loud while I assemble sources… Here's a first pass. The most directly relevant body of work is the chronotype × intervention literature; I'll prioritize that and bring in a couple of negative results to keep the picture honest. I added 3 new sources to the panel on the right. Want me to dig into any of them in particular? What are the specific methodological limitations of the Newport & Hempel study? observation.title: Lumen Research — research assistant
observation.visible_text: Lumen + New thread TODAY Deep work scheduling literature EV battery recycling policy in Norway Trace prevalence of seal influenza H10N7 LAST 7 DAYS Comparative grad-school stipends in CS Microclimate effects of urban rooftop gardens Late-Holocene shoreline shifts, NW Europe Why does ringing happen in step responses EARLIER Survey: open-source funding models 2024 Caffeine half-life in slow metabolizers Building codes vs wildfire defensible space PA Priya Anand Researcher · Pro Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." Can you summarize the key findings from the Newport & Hempel study mentioned in point 3? L Thinking out loud while I assemble sources… Here's a first pass. The most directly relevant body of work is the chronotype × intervention literature; I'll prioritize that and bring in a couple of negative results to keep the picture honest. I added 3 new sources to the panel on the right. Want me to dig into any of them in particular? What are the specific methodological limitations of the Newport & Hempel study? observation.title: Lumen Research — research assistant
observation.visible_text: Lumen + New thread TODAY Deep work scheduling literature EV battery recycling policy in Norway Trace prevalence of seal influenza H10N7 LAST 7 DAYS Comparative grad-school stipends in CS Microclimate effects of urban rooftop gardens Late-Holocene shoreline shifts, NW Europe Why does ringing happen in step responses EARLIER Survey: open-source funding models 2024 Caffeine half-life in slow metabolizers Building codes vs wildfire defensible space PA Priya Anand Researcher · Pro Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." Can you summarize the key findings from the Newport & Hempel study mentioned in point 3? L Thinking out loud while I assemble sources… Here's a first pass. The most directly relevant body of work is the chronotype × intervention literature; I'll prioritize that and bring in a couple of negative results to keep the picture honest. I added 3 new sources to the panel on the right. Want me to dig into any of them in particular? What are the specific methodological limitations of the Newport & Hempel study? What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." Can you summarize the key findings from the Newport & Hempel study mentioned in point 3? L Thinking out loud while I assemble sources… Here's a first pass. The most directly relevant body of work is the chronotype × intervention literature; I'll prioritize that and bring in a couple of negative results to keep the picture honest.
